title: Follow the Sun
hook: Your fintech, Meridian, just got licences for India, Europe and the US in a single week. The board wants users everywhere to get fast responses and never lose a transaction.
context: Fintech with a single-region primary database expanding to three regions.
solution_brief: Give each account one home region for writes, handle replication lag with read-your-writes, use idempotent ledger sagas for cross-region transfers, fence old leaders on failover, and shape replication around data residency. Home-region ownership avoids write conflicts. Read-your-writes via home-region reads or version tokens. Idempotent ledger steps and compensation, not cross-ocean locks. Consensus election with epoch fencing, explicit RPO. Residency-aware partitioning and replication.

steps.prompt: One primary database serves everyone, so users on other continents see 200 to 300 ms on every request. You want low latency everywhere without conflicting writes on the same account. Which data design do you choose?
steps.context_note: Reads are easy to copy closer to users. Writes are the hard part.

options.text: Let any region write any account, and merge conflicting writes afterwards.
Give each account a home region that owns its writes, with replicas elsewhere for reads and recovery.
Keep one region and put a CDN in front of the API.
Shard accounts by account number, placing each shard in whichever region has space.

steps.explanation: One writer per account removes conflicting writes by design, and nearby replicas keep reads fast. Letting every region write means someone has to resolve conflicts on money. Sharding without regard to where the user lives still sends many users across an ocean on every write. A user whose home region is far away still pays cross-region write latency, so the home region should be chosen close to the user.
steps.bottleneck_note: Avoid conflicts by design: one owner per piece of data beats clever merging.

steps.prompt: A user in India pays a bill, travels to Europe and opens the app. The EU region serves their balance from a replica that is 2 seconds behind, so the old balance appears. How should the app make sure users see their own recent writes?
steps.context_note: Replication from India to the EU replica is asynchronous, so the replica is always slightly behind the home region.

options.text: Show a notice that balances may take a few seconds to update.
Read balances and recent transactions from the home region, or only from a replica that has reached the user's last write.
Turn off the EU replica and send every read to the India primary.
Keep the last known balance on the user's device and show it first.

steps.explanation: A user's own balance must never go backwards, so those reads go to the owner or wait until a replica has caught up to a version token from the write. Less critical reads can still use lagging replicas. Sending every read to India removes the latency benefit for everything else, and a device copy goes stale as soon as another device or a credit changes the balance.
steps.bottleneck_note: Choose consistency per read: critical reads go to the owner or wait for catch-up.

steps.prompt: A user in India sends money to a user whose account is owned by the EU region. Two-phase commit with locks across both regions would block whenever the link between continents is slow or down. Which design moves the money safely?
steps.context_note: The two accounts now live in different regions, so one transfer touches two ledgers that cannot share a local transaction.

options.text: Run two-phase commit between the two ledgers with a long timeout for slow links.
Debit the sender into an in-flight state, send a uniquely identified credit event, and reverse the debit if the credit fails.
Credit the receiver first so they are never kept waiting, then debit the sender when confirmation arrives.
Call one global ledger from both regions and wait for it on every transfer.

steps.explanation: A saga with durable events, a unique transfer id and idempotent steps stays correct under retries and partitions, and the reversal covers a credit that can never complete. A long-timeout two-phase commit holds locks over an unreliable link, and crediting first can create money that is never paid for if the debit fails.
steps.bottleneck_note: Prefer idempotent steps with compensation to long distributed locks.

steps.prompt: The US primary became unreachable, so you promoted a replica in another region. The old primary was only partitioned, and it has reconnected still believing it is the leader, so two primaries now accept writes. What stops the old leader's writes from being accepted?
steps.context_note: A network partition, not a crash, made the old primary look dead, and it does not know it has been replaced.

options.text: Have the old primary poll the new one every few seconds and step down when it notices.
Number each leadership term with an increasing epoch and have storage reject writes carrying an older epoch.
Let both primaries accept writes and merge the conflicts once the partition heals.
Shut the old primary down by hand once someone sees the alert.

steps.explanation: Fencing makes the check at the storage layer, so a stale leader is refused no matter what it believes. Polling leaves a window in which it still accepts writes, and merging account balances afterwards risks lost or doubled money. Asynchronous replication can also lose the last few seconds of writes on failover, so the acceptable loss (RPO) must be decided in advance.
steps.bottleneck_note: Failover correctness is about fencing the old leader, not just promoting a new one.

steps.prompt: A regulator requires EU customers' personal and financial data to stay inside the EU, but your plan copies every account to every region for resilience. How should replication change?
steps.context_note: Resilience and residency pull in opposite directions: every extra region holding a copy is another place the rule applies.

options.text: Encrypt the replicated EU data and keep copies in every region.
Replicate EU accounts only to other EU locations, route users to their home region, and share only anonymised data globally.
Move all customer data to the US region as a single source of truth.
Keep full replication but strip names and emails from the copies outside the EU.

steps.explanation: Residency is a hard constraint, so the replication topology has to follow it: EU data replicates only to EU locations, which still gives disaster recovery inside the permitted geography. Encryption does not change where the data sits, and stripping names from the copies leaves balances and transactions that are still personal financial data.
steps.bottleneck_note: Legal constraints shape topology. Model them as part of the architecture, not afterwards.
